svg.text: THE PERIODIC TABLE, BY WHICH WAY IS DOWNHILL
The slope of the binding curve: violet to green elements still give energy by fusing, orange to red ones by splitting. It crosses zero at iron and nickel.
Iron to copper: the top (zero at A ≈ 62)
Hydrogen: the steepest climb of all
The binding curve, coloured by its slope
Slope of the binding curve (keV per nucleon, per nucleon added)
Violet to green: still climbing, so fusing gives energy. Orange to red: past the top, so splitting does.
Greyish yellow: the top. Each side has its own scale; the light side is far steeper.
Solid lines: periods. Dashed: groups. Dots sit where the chart puts
each element: atomic size across, mass up (both logarithmic).
The slope is d(B/A)/dA: how much tighter each nucleon gets held if the
nucleus gains one more nucleon. It's smoothed (a liquid-drop fit to the
measured AME2020 values, A ≥ 16), so the shell bumps and helium's spike
are ironed out; the scale is compressed (asinh) to show both sides.
Each element is placed at its most abundant (or longest-lived) isotope.
Superheavy values (Z ≥ ~104) are AME2020 extrapolations, not measured.
Data: IAEA Nuclear Data Services LiveChart (AME2020 masses, NUBASE
abundances & half-lives); radii & masses as on the main chart.
